lede: Stations read against the page images of their sources only; each names its source and, where printed, links to its passage.

stations.text: A witness at the trial for the murder of Harrison T. Riley tells of a meeting in Jason Alford's house on the Saturday night before the killing: “That was a meeting of an organization known as the Sara Sota Vigilance Committee, styled S. S. V. C.”
stations.quelle: Bacon, Andrews and Bidwell v. State, 22 Fla. 51 (January term 1886), p. 64.

stations.text: Harrison T. Riley is shot on the road and his throat cut, on the orders, as members later testify, of the committee's “judges”.
stations.quelle: The Pensacolian, 31 January 1885, p. 4; Bacon v. State, 22 Fla. 51 (1886), p. 62.

stations.text: The Florida Mortgage and Investment Company announces “a provisional contract … for the purchase of 47,000 acres of freehold land, situate on Sarasota Bay, Manatee County, Florida”; the most delicate vegetables grown there go to the northern markets in January and February, “as the lands are below the frost line”.
stations.quelle: Prospectus, The Economist, 25 October 1884, p. 1313.

stations.text: Charles E. Abbe is killed by a shotgun shot to the head; Florida's Supreme Court later finds the killing premeditated and upholds the conviction of Joseph C. Anderson as present, aiding and abetting.
stations.quelle: Anderson v. State, 24 Fla. 139 (1888), p. 140.

stations.text: The press reports the arrests: “a society of thugs at Sarasota”, with judges, a captain and an oath; the prisoners are held at Pine Level, and the people were “with great difficulty” prevented from lynching them.
stations.quelle: The Pensacolian, 31 January 1885, p. 4, after the Florida Times-Union.

stations.text: At a special term of the Circuit Court for Manatee County the jury finds Edmond P. Bacon guilty of the murder of Harrison T. Riley, and Leonard F. Andrews and Alfred B. Bidwell guilty as accessories; Adam W. Hunter is acquitted.
stations.quelle: Bacon, Andrews and Bidwell v. State, 22 Fla. 51 (1886), pp. 52–53.

stations.text: A neighbour from Sarasota, in Buffalo: “Sara Soto is no town. It is only a frontier settlement. … There never was any formal organization known as the Sara Soto Assassination society.”
stations.quelle: The Atlanta Constitution, 27 July 1885, editorial page, after the Buffalo Express.

stations.text: The promoter J. S. Tait writes from “Ormiston”: the colonists, “upwards of 100 souls”, arrived “in excellent health”; the natives are spreading “false rumors”.
stations.quelle: Chicago Daily Tribune, 6 February 1886, p. 5.

stations.text: A colonist remembers: “About January 9 it became much colder and snow began to fall, greatly to the surprise of the natives who thought at first the woods were afire and that the ashes were being carried by the wind.”
stations.quelle: Memoirs of Alex Browning, as quoted in Karl H. Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 97.

stations.text: A colonist's diary: “The colony seems to have completely broken up.” Three days later: “any place is better than desolate Sarasota.”
stations.quelle: Diary of Dan McKinlay, in Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 98.

stations.text: The state gazetteer lists Sarasota as “a recently established settlement and post office” that “has no present business interest to report”.
stations.quelle: Florida State Gazetteer and Business Directory 1886–87, s.v. Sarasota.

stations.text: The company's hotel opens with a ball: “More than two hundred persons attended and the party lasted until daybreak the next morning.”
stations.quelle: Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 106.

stations.text: A London monthly counts Sarasota among the “Scottish failures in attempting to colonise a region utterly unsuited for them” — and adds: “Florida has had booms before and will have them again.”
stations.quelle: W. R. Lawson, Time (London), April 1887, pp. 479–480.

stations.text: The building boom is over; the company asks $10 or more an acre and finds no buyers.
stations.quelle: Grismer (1946), p. 113.

stations.text: The last rail is laid on the Sarasota division of the railroad from Braidentown; the next day a flat car with a top carries the first party down the line.
stations.quelle: Manatee River Journal, 25 February 1892, p. 2.

stations.text: The county school board lists “A. C. Hudson, Sarasota, colored” among its teachers.
stations.quelle: Manatee River Journal, 11 October 1894, p. 3.

stations.text: The second freeze of the winter: “The mercury plummeted to 14.” Groves south of the Manatee River survive better than those farther north.
stations.quelle: Grismer (1946), p. 120; Manatee River Journal, 14 March 1895.

stations.text: A directory of the people living in what became Sarasota County lists the residents of Sarasota by name. “Six colored persons also were listed: J. Coleman, Lewis Colson, E. Justice, John Mays, and I. P. and W. S. Washington.”
stations.quelle: Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 131, after a directory of 1897.

stations.text: At a mass meeting in Harry L. Higel's office on the wharf the village votes to incorporate as a town. “Practically every qualified voter in the village attended—53 of them.”
stations.quelle: Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 136.

stations.text: The first train of the Seaboard's subsidiary arrives at 8 p.m.; the tracks run on to a dock where fish houses are built.
stations.quelle: Grismer (1946), p. 135.

stations.text: The legislature passes a bill “legalizing the incorporation of the town of Sarasota”.
stations.quelle: Manatee River Journal, 24 April 1903, p. 4.

stations.titel: The circus man buys a home
stations.text: John Ringling, fishing in the Sarasota section, buys the winter home of C. N. Thompson, “said to be one of the finest places in that section of the State”.
stations.quelle: Tampa Times, 28 August 1911, reprinted in the Manatee River Journal, 31 August 1911, p. 1.

stations.text: On 33rd Street, outside the town, Black families build “tiny homes” in Newtown, opened by Charles N. Thompson. “Previously, their principal living quarters had been at Black Bottom, in the vicinity of 12th and Lemon.”
stations.quelle: Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 179.

stations.text: Harry L. Higel, three times mayor, is found dying on Siesta Key. When a suspect is brought to Sarasota, “a mob began gathering. A rope was hurriedly secured”; the sheriff takes him to Bradenton. He is released; the murder is never solved.
stations.quelle: Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), pp. 202–203.

stations.text: Committees in Bradentown agree on the line: “All north of this boundary to remain as Manatee county, and all south to become Sarasota county.”
stations.quelle: Manatee River Journal, 5 May 1921, p. 1.

stations.text: J. R. Bunkley, “former convict guard, who is being held for the murder of a negro prisoner at Salt Springs”, is bound over on a bond of $5,000 until the grand jury of Sarasota County meets. In the same week the Governor appoints the officials of the new county.
stations.quelle: Manatee River Journal, 23 June 1921, p. 1.

stations.text: A hurricane comes ashore north of Tampa. At Sarasota the fish houses, the railroad dock, boats and nets and most of the municipal pier are destroyed.
stations.quelle: Monthly Weather Review, October 1921, p. 570; Grismer (1946), p. 204.

stations.text: A booklet sets “the great goal”: “a city of twenty-five thousand permanent residents within the next five years”.
stations.quelle: Sarasota: A City of Glorified Opportunity (about 1924), p. [4].

stations.text: “Approximately 150 local Klansmen attended the circus in full Klan regalia. A huge Klan parade was held immediately before the start of the evening's program.”
stations.quelle: Sarasota Herald, 17 November 1925, p. 7.
stations.citeLabel: The colour line in the boom [3]

stations.text: The Klan advertises in the Sarasota Herald: it stands for “LAW and ORDER … White Supremacy and Protestant Christianity”.
stations.citeLabel: The colour line in the boom [4]
stations.quelle: Sarasota Herald, 29 November 1925, p. 8.

stations.text: John Ringling's causeway to St. Armands and Lido opens to the public; homesites from $3,000, concerts by the Czecho-Slovakian National Band.
stations.quelle: Grismer (1946), pp. 212–213; Sarasota Herald, 19 February 1926, p. 24.

stations.text: Six men from Newtown are jailed after arguing whether “the new negro quarters, should be included in Greater Sarasota”.
stations.citeLabel: The colour line in the boom [5]
stations.quelle: Sarasota Herald, 18 August 1926, p. 5.

stations.titel: A hotel for the colored tourist trade
stations.text: E. O. Burns announces a $15,000 hotel on Central near Fourteenth Street that “will cater to the colored tourist trade”, to be named for Louis Colson, who had worked in the home of J. H. Gillespie and died about two years before.
stations.quelle: Sarasota Herald, 18 August 1926, p. 5.
stations.citeLabel: The colour line in the boom [6]

stations.text: Drained from 1924 and first planted in January 1927, Palmer Farms sends its first shipment: three cars of tomatoes and one of potatoes. It later turns to celery; by 1946 “70 per cent of those employed are negroes”.
stations.quelle: Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 256.

stations.text: The census counts 8,398 people in the city of Sarasota, against 2,149 in 1920 and 840 in 1910, and 12,440 in Sarasota County.
stations.quelle: Fifteenth Census of the United States: 1930, Population, vol. I, Florida, table 4, p. 213.

stations.text: The Army air base, a bomber base from the spring of 1942 and then a fighter base with more than 3,000 men at its peak, is inactivated; the following month the government turns it back to the Airport Authority.
stations.quelle: Grismer, The Story of Sarasota (1946), p. 250.
